title: 🐾 Peoples of the Second Age III — Eight Animal Peoples, Orc Absence & Living Mountains
rawNotionMarkup: Second Age people-by-people annals, Part III: eight animal-featured peoples, plus two important historical limits. These are newly developed revisable local histories, not species-wide destinies. Animal resemblance does not determine morality, profession, family size, instincts or birth rates. Avarran era names are only historian's cross-reference labels, not the names other continents are required to use. ## Wolvenkin — the boundary of loyalty Years 1–321: Some Wolvenkin households joined coldland and highland rescue circuits, though many lived in cities, fields and coastal towns. the House of Unrelated Guests was a refuge founded by Enna Frost-Veil, a Wolvenkin carpenter, after a local magistrate tried to forbid feeding strangers during a ration crisis. Her relatives disagreed: several feared the home would be emptied before their own children could eat. She established a counted common store and permitted neighbors to inspect it. The refuge survived through a hard winter, but it strained families, took sacrifices and never resolved everyone's fears. Other Wolvenkin communities followed different loyalties and legal customs. Years 322–1,321: Newly mastered lunar signaling and healing enabled independent scouts, physicians and artisans to serve market and mountain routes. the Grey-Pass Treason Case concerned a Wolvenkin guard accused of betraying his employer after warning a rival village of an approaching avalanche. A military tribunal initially convicted him; pressure from rescue crews forced an appeal. The revised ruling recognized a limited duty to warn civilians of immediate natural danger. The story became a challenge to the assumption that loyalty means obeying leaders at any human cost. Years 1,322–1,437: Northern rescue groups and frontier households in the existing Era of Fire chronicle developed independently; not every Wolvenkin was a scout or soldier. ## Foxfolk — a contract can deceive or protect Years 1–321: Foxfolk farmers, couriers, river merchants and urban families learned to verify changing magical claims against tangible goods. Terin Needle-Quill, a Foxfolk market clerk, exposed a warehouse group that sold enchanted food preservation to poor households but concealed the danger of failure. Several victims still lost their stored food, and the merchants were ordered to pay partial restitution only after repeated petitions. Terin's profession did not define Foxfolk as clever tricksters; many neighbors rejected his clerical career entirely. Years 322–1,321: Some Foxfolk communities cultivated scholarship in illusion appraisal, public contracts, performance and mediation. the Red-Silk Arbitration asked whether a trader could revoke a sale made after an enchantment concealed a fabric defect. Different judges disagreed; a compromise required open disclosure of magical modification at participating fairs. Wealthy patrons evaded the rule by moving business elsewhere, while honest factors built stronger reputations. Foxfolk could be villains, victims or reformers individually without sharing a species nature. Years 1,322–1,437: Foxfolk appear in scattered courts and trading families; the later Era of Fire's political changes did not impose one worldwide code. ## Lionfolk — duty beyond the gate Years 1–321: In Sahradi savannas and several cities elsewhere, Lionfolk households debated whether a respected family's duty ended at its own gate. At the Burned Orchard Judgment, a noble household refused to release stored water after a local magical garden failed. A Lionfolk farmer, Kadesh White-Brow, challenged the noble's claim that honor required protecting only ancestors' property. His testimony helped win emergency access for vulnerable residents, though a rival land court overturned similar measures. Some Lionfolk rulers were exploitative; some commoners upheld the very privileges that oppressed them. Years 322–1,321: Schools of law, healing, debate and magical protection developed in selected regions. the Quiet Standard Debate arose after an acclaimed military patron punished a Lionfolk healer for treating enemy prisoners. The healer's patients survived, and local advocates won a change in that city's custody rules. The patron kept his estates. This was hard-won legal dignity, not proof that all Lionfolk valued a single honor ethic or that every human conflict was compassionate. Years 1,322–1,437: Individual Lionfolk advisors and water-law advocates could participate in the Blue-Jar era without being defined by it. ## Tigerfolk — learning without a patron Years 1–321: Across Orundel's forest rivers and cities, Tigerfolk observers compared physical tracks, water heights and plant growth with increasingly untrustworthy divination. Selka of the Rain Lines, a Tigerfolk fieldworker, found that a powerful college's lunar flood prediction had been copied without local measurements. The ensuing flood devastated smaller river villages. Her insistence that paid scholars must listen to local observers produced the Field Note Hearing in one town. Other institutions rejected the finding to protect prestige. Years 322–1,321: Tigerfolk physicians, artists, engineers, civil servants, sailors and scholars belonged to competing schools of new lunar practice. the Thirty-Four Leaves Clinic used careful botanical records to compare magical and ordinary treatments; some healing claims failed, and the clinic publicly named those failures rather than hiding them. A donor attempted to suppress results that embarrassed his household. Students carried copies to traveling healers. This was an institutional triumph of honesty, not a biological Tigerfolk gift for science. Years 1,322–1,437: Orundel's separate War of Three Locks belongs to the late Second Age; not every Tigerfolk had any part in it. ## Elephantfolk — water belongs to the living too Years 1–321: Elephantfolk households and mixed civic councils kept flood marks and canal measurements, extending existing water stewardship traditions. the Old Basin Protest followed a noble's decision to divert water from tenant families to an enchanted ornamental reservoir. Matron Veysa of the North Canal, an Elephantfolk pottery merchant, carried household records to a public hearing and argued that unpaid repair labor created legitimate water rights. The dispute ended in a temporary distribution order; the lord attempted to reverse it. The conflict taught courts that memory was evidence only when accompanied by accountable measures, not an infallible species trait. Years 322–1,321: Irrigation schools, medicine, history and environmental lunar magic flourished in selected Elephantfolk civic circles. the Clay-Tally School trained students from several peoples to keep public flood and debt records without requiring noble sponsorship. A magistrate destroyed the school's first ledger after it exposed fraud; residents restored entries from household copies. Elephantfolk were also farmers, scholars, performers, traders and ordinary parents—never all communal engineers. Years 1,322–1,437: Sahrad's later Blue-Jar water-law culture and Jar Hearings drew on a region of long debate, but not every ancient Elephantfolk institution was one kingdom's property. ## Bearfolk — the work of shelter Years 1–321: Among coldland settlements, several Bearfolk families opened roadside shelters that used ordinary firewood, durable roofs and protected stores while certain magical heating systems failed. the Seven Empty Cots became a local memorial to travelers who died after a lord closed a refuge to outsiders. A Bearfolk innkeeper, Bruni Rainshelter, organized a new community shelter and persuaded rival households to contribute repair labor. Some declined and others tried to claim ownership. Her shelter continued because many citizens gave small amounts reliably, not because everyone shared her kindness. Years 322–1,321: Winter medicine, craft and newly mastered protective lunar arts supported prosperous communities. the Furrow-and-Fire Suit challenged an industrial guild that forced laborers into dangerous winter shifts without paying for warmth. A Bearfolk lawyer and Human textile workers secured a limited obligation to maintain safe shelters. Several mines changed practice; others secretly ignored it. Bearfolk were not assigned universal hibernation, fierceness, or fixed homeland, and several families led urban artistic lives. Years 1,322–1,437: The later Frost-Hearth Confederation and Blue-Snow House traditions intersect regionally, not by decree over every Bearfolk. ## Cowfolk — land is not a commandment Years 1–321: Cowfolk farming cooperatives helped certain mixed towns maintain soil fertility, seed stocks and reliable fodder without depending on unpredictable agricultural lunar magic. the Reedfield Council allowed tenant families to pool grain and contest estate owners who tried to confiscate seed after failed spells. Its first chair, Oren Larksedge, a Cowfolk town clerk who had never owned a farm, opposed the assumption that only landowners understood rural hardship. His proposal passed narrowly and later attracted urban merchants. Years 322–1,321: Magical agriculture and ordinary crop rotation encouraged wealth in some districts, while wealthy landlords expanded estates and displaced tenants elsewhere. the Uncut Field Lawsuit centered on land cultivated by mixed Cowfolk, Halfling and Human households but claimed by a noble because moon-born growth magic had been financed from his treasury. A city court recognized tenant improvements and required compensation, but the victims had already lost a season's harvest. Cowfolk citizens also pursued scholarship, legal work, military service, music and nonfarm trades. Years 1,322–1,437: Cattle, fields and ordinary urban life continue throughout the region's varied polities; no modern population number or inherited caste is backdated. ## Pigfolk — the ordinary dignity of a workshop Years 1–321: Pigfolk cooks, repair workers, urban residents and market families maintained sanitation, fuel systems and cooperative kitchens during uneven magical failure. the Smokehouse Ledger in a small town recorded unpaid service by women, apprentices and servants whom powerful families had omitted from public relief rolls. A Pigfolk apprentice, Hemi Wickerpan, risked prosecution by displaying the list in the town square. The council began distributing some food according to work and need rather than prestige, but accusations of favoritism survived. Years 322–1,321: New lunar arts enriched medicine, fine instruments, food production and machinery where people had resources to adopt them. the Copper Ladle Revolt broke out when a guild bound independent kitchen workers to its enchanted preservation equipment through ruinous rental contracts. Neighborhood buyers, including Pigfolk, Human and Goblin families, supported an alternative cooperative. It won the right to maintain nonmagical public ovens alongside licensed devices. Its cooperative later quarreled over revenue, proving that a just cause does not prevent future disagreements. Years 1,322–1,437: Pigfolk livelihoods and households continued in diverse ancient settlements; the era's dark mage history does not make animal-featured peoples inherently aligned with any magic. ## Urakai / Orcs — absent First and entire Second Ages: Urakai did not exist. There were no Orc villages, armies, clans, royal houses, alliances, treaties, magical schools, or wars in Second Age Eryndor, including all three Avarran eras. The exiled mages of southeastern Avarra created the Orcs sometime during the Third Age by an unknown means, with ambitions first to besiege Khazari strongholds and eventually attack Eldar and Human kingdoms. Their degree of control and whether specific attacks happened is undecided. Goblin and Ogre histories above are independent; any Orc-era alliances or east–west wars involving Orcs cannot predate the Third Age. ## Living Mountains — their history remains a true mystery Second Age: Rare sentient Living Mountains exist in Eryndor's broader setting, but their confirmed presence, activity, number and identities in the Second Age are not established. Later tales of a mountain that mourned the broken moons, sheltered a village or whispered warnings are possibilities for future stories, not factual Second Age sightings. They are not to be equated with the already-ancient Ironspine mountain ring, and their existence cannot be used to explain the worldwide earthquakes of Second Age Year 1,437 without an explicit new creator decision. ## Three enduring rules Survival is not innocence: no species went extinct at the global earthquakes ending the Second Age, but the destruction of settlements and loss of individual lives was vast. The magical contribution to species survival remains unestablished in mechanism. Magic is plural: the independent World's Breath continues alongside lunar magics; certain original moon-derived arts were permanently lost and cannot be recovered by simply studying a new moon. The Age's dramatic progress occurred within those limits. Lives are personal: no race is uniformly good, evil, familial, solitary, scholarly, martial, mercantile or servile. New rulers and local polities in these annals do not establish ancestry for Gloin Hammerfeld, origin dates for modern kingdoms, or present-day population counts.
